title: Car Sharing Business
desc: Plan a small car-sharing or ride-sharing service: legal checks, insurance, booking, safety, pricing and fairness to drivers and riders.
outcomes: Explain models: peer-to-peer, fleet and carpool.
Set up booking, ID and insurance steps.
Compute cost per hour and per km.
task: Design a small car-sharing service with legal checks, driver and rider vetting, booking flow, insurance, pricing and safety plan.
condition: A computer, a spreadsheet, a practice case, two peers and a mentor. Real vehicles or riders are not used.
standard: Legal and insurance checks are listed with sources; cost per km is correct; vetting and safety steps are written; fairness rules for drivers are included; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Entrepreneurs, community groups, fleet staff, employers with commute schemes.
evidence: legal checklist, booking flow, cost sheet, safety plan, launch plan
modules: Models of sharing
Understand
There are several ways to share cars.
Peer-to-peer lets owners rent their cars to others.
A fleet owned by an operator is booked by the hour.
Carpooling matches people with seats to riders.
Each model has different legal, insurance and trust needs.
Ask which model fits your community: trust, density and parking all matter.
Peer-to-peer needs strong identity checks; fleets need capital.
A residential building runs a shared car booked by the hour for members. A rural village with few cars chooses carpooling first because it needs no vehicles.
Compare three models in a table. Add a model choice with reasons.
Pros and cons for each.
Legal and insurance
Apply
Do not skip this.
Licences, vehicle checks, tax and permits.
Insurance that covers sharing, not only private use.
Written terms for damage and fines.
Data and privacy rules for location data.
Ask insurers in writing what is covered for sharing and what is excluded.
Check commercial licence rules for charging fees.
A policy covers hire use only if declared; an undeclared sharing claim is refused. An insurer confirms cover only for registered, declared vehicles and named drivers.
Make a legal checklist. Record an insurer's written answer or a practice case.
Each item has a source.
Vetting and identity
Apply
Know who drives.
Check licence and ID; set minimum experience.
Photo of vehicle before and after.
Privacy rules for data.
Block risky drivers.
Re-check licences regularly and block expired ones.
Offer a trial drive for new members.
A licence check fails and booking is blocked until the user provides valid documents. A monthly licence expiry report blocks three members until they upload new documents.
Write the vetting steps. Add a monthly vetting routine.
Steps are clear.
Booking and handover
Apply
Make the journey smooth and fair.
App or form: choose car, time and deposit.
Digital or key handover; fuel or charge rule.
Late and cancel rules.
Support line.
Use a deposit and a late fee to protect availability.
Photograph fuel or charge level at pickup and return.
A checklist records mileage and damage at pickup and return. A 2,000 INR deposit is held and released within 48 hours of a clean return.
Design the flow. Draw the flow with times.
Flow has eight steps.
Costs and price
Analyse
Know the real cost per hour and per km.
Fixed: insurance, depreciation, parking. Variable: fuel, wear.
Cost per hour and per km.
Utilisation for break-even.
Review regularly.
Compare cost per hour for 2, 4 and 8 hour bookings.
Show members an example bill before they book.
Fixed cost 520 INR per day plus 7 INR per km; at 80 km a day, cost per km is 13.5 INR. A 4-hour trip of 40 km costs 130 INR fixed share plus 280 INR distance cost.
Build a cost sheet. Test the sheet with three trips.
Currency shown.
Safety and incidents
Evaluate
Plan for problems.
Breakdown, accident and fraud steps.
Emergency numbers and first aid kit.
Incident log and review.
Roadside help.
List emergency contacts in the car and the app.
Run a mock breakdown with a tow call.
A driver reports a flat tyre; roadside help is called and the booking extended. A tow and a replacement car are arranged within 90 minutes in the mock run.
Write an incident plan. Run and time a mock incident.
Steps ordered.
Fairness and community
Evaluate
Treat all fairly.
No discrimination in access.
Fair rates and clear fees.
Accessibility options.
Feedback loop.
Publish clear rules for cancellations and damage.
Offer a pay-by-month option for low-income members.
A rule offers hand controls on request and trains staff. A fee cap and an appeal route make the service fairer.
List fairness rules. Add a fee cap and appeal route.
Rules clear.
Launch plan
Create
Test small.
Pilot with one car and 20 members.
Track use, damage and feedback.
Improve.
Decide to grow.
Define pilot metrics: utilisation, damage per 100 trips, member score.
Set a review at day 30 and day 90.
Pilot: 60 per cent utilisation and 1 minor damage. Pilot: 60 per cent utilisation, 1 minor damage and a score of 4.4 after 30 days.
Present the plan. Set your targets.
Peers follow.
